newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar fall; bonds up as gold hits 12-year lows.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar fall; bonds up as gold hits 12-year lows.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell sharply Monday as investors took profits after last week's powerful rally.
Bonds rose as gold prices plunged to new 12-year lows as Australia's central bank sold large amounts of the precious metal.
The dollar fell against the yen after Japan said its preliminary June trade surplus more than doubled from last year.
The 30-share Dow fell 37.32 points to 7,858.49 as investors paused after a blistering three-session run that put the blue-chip index in record territory.
Early in the session, the Dow appeared set to move above 8,000 as it surged as high as 7,951 in the opening hour of trading. But, just as quickly, the rally ran out of steam.

Last week, the blue-chip index jumped 209 points after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady and new employment and wage data offered further evidence that economic growth was moderating and inflation remained at bay.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,457 to 1,397 on active volume of 518 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The market's entitled to a little rest," said Al Goldman, an analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "We've had a one-way trip up."
Analysts attributed much of the retreat to routine profit-taking, noting many declining issues were among those that racked up big gains last week.
Few analysts thought the drop represented anything more than a brief interruption in the sizzling run that has left most, if not all, of Wall Street's forecasts far behind.
"The bulls are definitely still in charge here," said Greg Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities Inc. "Any profit-taking here is likely to be resonably contained and very short-term."

Particularly weak were gold mining stocks, which tumbled along with bullion prices, which sank to a fresh 12-year low, as speculators worried about recent gold sales by central banks. The August gold contract fell $6.20 to $319 an ounce, a level unseen since 1985 on New York's Commodity Exchange.
The 30-year Treasury rose 20/32, or $6.25 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.58 percent from 6.61 percent Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar dipped below 112 yen before steadying in New York at 112.83 yen, compared with 113.82 late Thursday.
After falling more than a pfennig, the dollar trimmed its losses to 1.7530 marks, down a touch from 1.7535 Thursday.

Meanwhile, wheat prices fell to three-year lows and corn prices hit 2-1/2-year lows as the ideal growing weather in the United States pointed to bumper -- and possibly record -- crops. At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for July delivery
closed down 6-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.13-1/2.
In corn, the largest grain crop, the main futures contract for harvest delivery, December, closed at $2.29-1/2, down 4 cents after setting a new life-of-contract low.

Soybeans for harvest delivery also fell with November futures ending down 7-3/4 cents a bushel at $5.84-1/4. But the July delivery bucked the lower trend on concerns that soybeans remaining for cash delivery may be squeezed.
July soybeans ended at $7.32-3/4, up 10-3/4 cents.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended lower on concerns that Iraq will soon submit its aid distribution plan to the United Nations and resume exporting oil under its accord with the United Nations.
Crude oil for August delivery closed 4 cents lower at $19.52 a barrel. Monday's decline followed a 78-cent decline in crude in Thursday's session on the same concerns.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,810.7, down 2.1 points, or 0.04 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 19,705.17, down 262.83 points, or 1.32 percent.
